speechtext: For the production of the original papers, letters, memoranda, and other documents, comprising file No. 762a, being the file quoted from by the Minister of Public Works on Tuesday, April 17, 1913?

subtopic: PRODUCTION OF ORIGINAL AND PRIVATE PAPERS.
speechtext: While personally I have no objection to bring down the file as asked for, I would like to have it made clear, whether in so doing I would be in keeping with any precedent of this House heretofore established under similar conditions. The file referred to contained certain private documents, some of which were read in the House by myself, and of which I furnished copies to be laid upon the table. If my hon. friend wants the original documents, and will amend his motion, I shall be very glad to bring them down. If it is in accordance with the rules of the Plouse, I have no objection td place in charge of the clerk the file referred to in its entirety.

subtopic: PRODUCTION OF ORIGINAL AND PRIVATE PAPERS.
speechtext: Within the knowledge of a number of hon. members, a precedent ha's been established that when original documents are produced they must be placed in charge of the clerk and subject to the custody of the clerk, so that the safety of the documents would be on the responsibility of officers of the House. There would be no question about that part of it. It is in accordance with that precedent that I have made the request for the original documents in this way. When my hon. friend was reading the correspondence, the question was argued before you, Mr. Speaker, as to whether or not the hon. minister should lay upon the table the whole of the file. You, Sir^ decided that it was not requisite that he should do so. The hon. minister himself at that time said that if I wanted the file I would get it by moving in the ordinary way. I afterwards asked the hon. minister for such information as would identify the file so that I would be able to move for its production. He gave me the information. I have moved for the production of the file, and I would respectfully urge that my motion be agreed to.

speechtext:
My recollection of the
incident is that the documents in that case were not brought down upon any motion, but were laid upon the table by my hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) at the conclu-son of the debate. I looked up the debate, and two motions were proposed by the Opposition. One was accepted by the Government and the other was rejected. The motion for the production of the original documents was also rejected. The motion which was accepted by the then Government was this:
Subject to suck consideration of public policy as can be validly urged in any case, it is the undoubted right of the people's representatives in Parliament assembled to be informed of everything necessary to explain the policy and proceedings of the Government and! for that purpose to have an opportunity of seeing and examining all documents connected! with the transaction of public business; and the denial of such right by the Government justifies the refusal of this House of further supplies to the Crown.
The documents were still not brought down, and a further motion was proposed by the hon. member for East Hastings (Mr. Northrup) as follows:
Subject to such consideration of public policy as can he validly urged in any case members of parliament have the right to have access to all the records of the Government and to all the archives.

This motion was rejected. At the conclusion of a somewhat heated debate, the Prime Minister, as will be seen at page 1927 of ' Hansard,' laid the papers upon the table. That was the course taken in that case. There is no objection to having these papers laid upon the _ table of the House, but I think they should be laid on the table in the same way, as in the case mentioned, namely, subject to their being returned to the department. When I say that they should be laid on the table of the House, of course that is subject to any consideration of public policy; and documents which it would not be in the public interest to bring down would not be brought down. This is in accordance with the course which was taken then, namely, that the Prime Minister laid the papers on the table of the House, and they were subject to being returned to the department. The Minister of the Interior of that day, my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) brought down in the first instance a somewhat elaborate document prepared by his deputy minister, which pointed out and emphasized the very great inconvenience of any original papers being taken out of a department. Of course, great inconvenience may be occasioned, but I imagine that all the documents required in this case can be brought down without any special inconvenience.	[DOT]

Consideration in Committee of Bill No. 21, to authorize measures for increasing the effective Naval Forces of the Empire- Mr. Borden-resumed from May 6. (Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair.)
On section 2:
From and out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada there may be paid and ap-lied a sum not exceeding thirty-five million dollars for the purpose of immediately increasing the effective naval forces of the Empire.
And the amendment thereto, proposed by Mr. German:
That clause 2 be struck out and that the following be substituted therefor:	Upon appropriations in that behalf being from time
to time made by Parliament, there may be paid and applied from and out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada a sum not exceeding $35,000,000 for the purpose of speedily increasing the effective naval forces of the Empire.

Mr. Chairman, before the debate was adjourned last night, I was trying to point out that the time had arrived when the Government should take the House and the country into its. confidence and give us more certain, definite information as to what its policy, in respect to naval defence, is going to be. I alluded to statements made by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Borden) on different occasions which, to the ordinary man, would seem to be inconsistent. I pointed out that on different occasions he had enunciated policies which, to my mind at all events, were irreconcilable. Perhaps a man of the fine psychological turn of the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. White), or of the hon member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen), might be able to show that these statements were not inconsistent and that the policy laid down by the Government has been quite reconcilable throughout, but to the hardheaded man the speeches made by the Prime Minister and other hon. gentlemen opposite on different occasions are not reconcilable. I also referred to the principles laid down by the Montreal Star as not being in harmony with the views expressed by hon. gentlemen opposite. It is time that the country should know definitely what is proposed to be done.
It is time, when we are asked for $35,000,000 to send over to the Old Country, when the old country is not in need of one dollar of it and when we in this country need every dollar of it for the development of our resources, that we should know what the intentions of the Government are. As far as the province of Nova Scotia is concerned, I can understand how far $35,000,000 would go in the way of removing some of the railway difficulties that we have. It would go a considerable way in redeeming some of the pledges made by hon. gentlemen opposite on the eve of the last election and upon another occasion since, in so far as providing accommodation is concerned. If you are going to send $35,000,000 this year what will it be next year and the year after? Will this sum be increased as we grow wealthier and more numerous and as the duties that are alleged become greater? Upon what principle is it proposed to make a gift of this $35,000,000? Is it that, when the Government is in a generous mood and has an overflowing treasury, we are to make a gift of this kind, or is it to be a regular contribution in recognition of the duty which we owe to the Mother Country in

return for the help and protection which we have received from her since we started out in business for ourselves? Then, we would like to know, if their policy is not a regular policy of contribution what is to be their permanent policy if they have such? It is all right to tell us that they propose to say later on-why not say it now? The people of the country have a right to know at this time what the Government propose to do.
The late Government embarked upon a policy, they passed the Laurier Naval Act, that policy was approved by both parties and was referred to by the right hon. Prime Minister himself, in England, and in various parts of Canada, as a proper policy to embark upon and one that should commend itself, nut only to every patriotic Canadian, but also to every Englishman. Hon. gentlemen opposite have promised to repeal that Naval Act and they have already begun to destroy any effect that it might have had. They have taken steps to allow the sailors on the training ships to leave those vessels and they are practically putting these vessels out of commission. What we ask them to do is to come out honestly and above board and tell us frankly what they have in mind in this respect. I submit that the statements which have been made by the Prime Minister on various occasions justify me in saying that his position is one which the country cannot understand. Let me quote a few of the utterances of the right hon. gentleman. First, let me refer to his statement at page 24 of the pamphlet, containing his speech of the 5th December, which has been scattered broadcast throughout the country. On the 5th of December he said:
There have been proposals, to which I shall no more than allude, that we should build uip a great naval organization in Canada. In my humble opinion, nothing of an efficient character could be built up in this country within a quarter or perhaps half a century. Even then it would be but a poor and weak substitute for the splendid organization which the Empire already possesses, which has been evolved and built up through centuries of the most searching experience and of the highest endeavour. Is there really any need that we should undertake the hazardous and costly experiment of building up a naval organization especially restricted to this Dominion, when upon just and self-respecting terms we can take such part as we desire in naval defence through the existing naval organization of the Empire, and in that way fully and effectively avail ourselves of the men and the resources at the command of Canada ?
What inference are we to draw from the language used by the Prime Minister on that occasion? Is it not clearly a condemnation of the Canadian naval policy? It is true that his language is somewhat equivocal, it is true that he does not expressly Mr. CHISHOLM (Antigonish).
condemn the Canadian naval policy, but what is the ordinary man to understand from such language as that? It is that the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite is not a policy of building up a Canadian navy, but rather one of utilising an organization which he said was available to us upon terms consistent with our dignity as a self-respecting, independent colony of the Empire, but which terms, as I showed last night, have no real existence in fact. Let me quote further his utterances on the 27th February last as reported at page 4269 of ' Hansard.' They aTe as follows:
What will be the purpose of the navy which my hon. friends propose to create when it is created ? They propose to have one fleet unit on the Atlantic and one fleet unit on the Pacific. For what purpose will they be placed there and to what extent will they be effective? I say that the best defence of Canada will be by the united naval forces of the whole Empire; and I further maintain that it would he impossible for a single fleet unit on the Atlantic, or a single fleet unit on the Pacific, to defend the shores or coast line of Canada against such an attack as might be expected, if tan attack were to take place.
I submit that the only conclusion you would draw from these remarks of the Prime Minister of the 27th February is that he is not in favour of a Canadian navy, that he sees no necessity for it whatsoever, that Canada now has all the navy she requires, namely, the British navy, and that the duty devolves upon Canada to contribute to that navy in the North sea. Let me now quote, in contra-distinction to these statements, other statements, and I do this for the purpose of showing that in view of his seemingly irreconcilable attitude, in view of his variety of policies from time to time, now that he is asking for this money, the country has a right to know definitely what he means, and is justified in asking that he make a candid statement of the policy which he proposes. Let me quote the language which he used in Halifax when he enunciated his policy there. He said in Halifax cn the 14th October, 1909, that:
The House of Commons, last session, laid down a certain policy touching naval defence in which both nolitical parties united.
It may not have the aspirations of aXI' Conservatives, hut it seemed our bounden' duty to place, if possible, above the limits of partisan strife a question so vital and far-reaching, and to attain the standard which has for many years governed both political parties in Great Britain with respect to foreign nations.
If the policy annouuneed in 1908 may not have satisfied the aspirations of all Conservatives, as the Prime Minister said, I wonder if there is anything in the vague indistinct policy which he now has that

will satisfy the aspirations of all Conservatives, or that will appeal to the manhood of Canada and make us proud of the stock from which we have sprung. The right hon. gentleman continued to say:
How the present Administration will work out the policy which was outlined by a resolution to which I have alluded, remains to be seen. One governing principle at least should control, namely, that out of our own materials, by our own labour and by the instructed skill of our own people any neces-i sary provision for our naval defences should be made so far as may be reasonably possible. In this connection may we not hope that there shall be given a stimulus and encouragement to the ship-building industry of Canada which has long been lacking.
In 1909 he had no doubt whatever of the aspirations of the people and he knew that Liberals and Conservatives alike desired a policy that would involve the using of our own material by our own labour and by the constructive skill of our own people. He stated further:
To-day should be Nova Scotia's opportunity in that regard. Providence has endowed this province with the material, with the men, and with the maritime situation which are essential not only for developing a scheme of naval defence and protection, but also for the resuscitation of this ship-building industry which once made Nova Scotia famous throughout the world.
There is no suggestion of contribution in that statement. How is the right hon. gentlemen going to revive the ship-building industry by sending away $35,000,000 this year and perhaps a greater sum in future years? Speaking at Toronto on November 1, 1909, the right hon. gentleman is reported as follows:
Mr. Borden spoke with great deliberation and evidently weighed his words carefully. He unhesitatingly reaffirmed his adherence to the naval defence policy outlined in the House of Commons resolution passed last March. Mr. Borden scouted the idea of Canada relying on the navy of the United States in time of danger, and characterized as absurd the plea that we are incapable of building a navy in this country.
What happened between 1909 and the visit of the Prime Minister to London last year, which leads him to think that now we are not able to build anything like a navy when in 1909 he scouted that idea. Speaking at a luncheon given at the Constitutional Club in London on Dominion Day, July 1, 1909, Mr. Borden is reported in the London Times of July 2, as having said:
He -was aware that some feeling was created in the British Isles owing to the fact that Canada did not by resolution or by speech from the Prime Minister, vouchsafe to offer one, two, or three dreadnoughts. He thought the resolution, in the form in which it was based, while its promises might not upon the
surface seem to some as significant at the moment as the offer of one or two dreadnoughts would have been, laid down a permanent policy for the Dominion of Canada upon -which both parties united and which would serve a more practical purpose than any such offer of dreadnoughts.
If the Prime Minister was correctly reported by the London Times, he lauded the Laurier Naval Act as the best naval permanent policy for the Dominion of Canada upon which both parties had united, and which would serve a more practical purpose than any offer of dreadnoughts. If the Laurier policy was a good permanent policy then, what has occurred since to change his mind? In view of the utterances of the Prime Minister on these various occasions, and in view of his statements then and his statements now, which to the ordinary hardheaded, commonsense man are irreconcilable, does not the Prime Minister owe it to himself, to his Government, to this House and to the country, to tell us simply and clearly what is to be his permanent policy if he has any. Last night the Prime Minister, to a question put by my hon. friend from King's, P.E.I. (Mr. Hughes) stated he had received hundreds of letters from Liberals who are dissatisfied and disgusted with the policy of the Liberal party on this question.

I would like to see some
of them.

Yes, it would be interesting to see some of them. I have seen that statement in the Halifax Herald, which is supposed to be the organ of the leader of the Government, and some of these telegrams appeared in that newspaper, but from my point of view none of the senders of these telegrams would pass as Liberals. We know that a Government in power is in the very poorest position to tell what is going on in the country; we know that the Government is not likely to hear any views and opinions of a critical character from those who are seeking favours. There is a class of persons who may write letters in the newspapers, signing themselves ' Old-time Liberals ' or ' Disaffected Liberals,' but if you scratch them you will find they are Tories of the simon-pure brand, or, in a rare instance there may be a disgruntled Liberal who did not get what he wanted. If we are to judge by what we hear travelling in the trains and in the corridors of hotels and other public places, I think the sentiment is overwhelmingly against the naval proposal of the present Government.
I have heard Conservatives from various parts of the country discussing this matter, and the general impression seems to be that the people of Canada do not enthuse over this mysterious naval policy of the 1 Conservative party. They do not approve

of sending $35,000,000 to the Old Country. They have faith in their country. They have been taught by the old leaders of the Conservative party that this country is as great as any other country in the world, and that anything that can be done in any other country can be done in Canada. They have been taught that there is no task too great for the people of Canada to undertake. As was pointed out very eloquently by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) when he spoke on this question in 1909, there is good reason why that should be the case. He stated that this policy of contribution was not one that would appeal to the majority of the people, because it did not strike root; it did not develop the Canadian sentiment or the pride that a Canadian naval policy would develop; it was too much like hiring a man to do for you what you ought to do for yourself. These are Mr. Foster's words on that occasion:
It bears the aspect of hiring somebody else to do what we ourselves ought to do. . . . In Canada itself there will be no roots struck, there will be no residue left, there will be no preparation of the soil or beginning of the growth of the product. ... It disjoins what
. has been joined together from the earliest days of the world's existence-commerce and the protection of commerce. . . .
He goes on to say:
. That method ignores the necessities, and the aspirations, and the prospects of a great people, such as the Canadian people are destined to become.
Then he went on to argue that, however humble our beginning may be, we should begin and that then was the time to make a beginning. He said that we must have something
In which Canada has some of her body, her bones, her blood, her mental power, and her national pride.
In those eloquent words, the member for North Toronto in 1909 expressed the aspirations of the people of Canada. I venture to say that the same sentiment prevails throughout the country to-day. The right hon. the Prime Minister referred last night to hundreds of letters which he had received from disaffected and disappointed Grits. He is perhaps in a worse position than anyone else to know what the real sentiment of the country is. He will naturally be beset by sycophants and flatterers, and assailed by those who have little axes to grind, and who pretend to see nothing but good in the action or policy of the Government. It would be interesting to know who those hundreds of Liberals are who are disgusted with the Liberal party. I saw in that bulwark of Conservatism, the Orange Sentinel, a short time ago, the following statement:
The following letter has been received by the secretary of Diamond L.O.B.L., No. 1474, from Ottawa:
Mr. CHISHOLM (Antigonish).
Allow me, through this, to acknowledge receipt of the resolutions passed by Diamond L.O.B.L., No. 1474, on 10th March, 1913, endorsing right hon. R. L. Borden's naval policy, &c., and expressing sympathy with the unionists of Ireland in their heroic struggle. On behalf of right hon. Mr. Borden and myself I thank your lodge sincerely for these expressions of their approval and words of encouragement.
Yours fraternally,
(Sgd.) T. S. Sproule.
Who is that?

I do not know who he is, but this is a letter sent from Ottawa. I do not think you will find many Liberals in that body. It is not consistent with Liberal-ims to stand up for a party that gives expression to utterances such as Mr. F. E. Smith and Sir Edward Carson gave expression to when they were going to dethrone the King some time ago if Home Rule were granted to Ireland by the Parliament of Great Britain. When I read this article, it occurred to me that perhaps it was from members of this body that these letters of congratulation were sent from Liberals expressing their great admiration for the conduct of the Government in suppressing free speech in Parliament, and in endeavouring to force through Parliament by closure a measure which does not find favour with Liberals, and with a large proportion of Conservatives if they were free to express their opinions.
What is the meaning of the letters 'L.O.B.L.'?

I am not in their
secrets. Let me quote something more moderate, something more temperate in tone, and something that should appeal to everybody in Canada. In discussing the naval policy of the Conservative party this article goes on to say:
But there is a great deal more than that involved in the Conservative policy.
That is, the question as to whether there should be a contribution from time to time or not:
It has a bearing upon the whole question of our country's destiny. The dream which we believe is cherished by the great mass of Canada's young manhood is that we should build up, in this northern zone, under the British Crown, a' free nation, facing the problems and discharging the responsibilities which nationhood involves. Among these responsibilities is that of providing for our own defence and deciding in what wars, if any, we should voluntarily engage. To send away money, which may be used in waging war over whose inception we can have no control, and which in some cases might appear to our people unrighteous, is to establish a precedent that might well be fatal to our( highest aspirations.
Such naval preparation as Canada majy make at this time should, in our humble judgment, be on a modest scale, proportioned

to our needs as a peace loving and peace seeking nation, whose fixed policy will be to submit such misunderstandings as may rise with other nations to the decision of a judicial tribunal rather than to the arbitrament of the sword. By thus providing for our own need we shall fulfil our responsibility as a component part of the Empire, while at the same time, we can, with consistency and a clear conscience, join in the attempt to bring the civilized nations together for the purpose of making international arbitration the fixed and universal rule.
I quote that from page 261 of the Presbyterian, a weekly review of church life and work. The paper is dated February 27, 1913. I think these are the true sentiments of the people of Canada from one end of the country to the other. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister, previous to December 5, last, stated in Montreal that if Parliament did not pass this measure he would go to the country, and he made the same statement during the course of his speech on December 5 last. At the time he made that statement he did not anticipate that this measure would be forced through the House of Commons by closure; I am sure that nothing of that kind occurred to him. What he meant was that this policy of his was so acceptable to the people at large that it would receive their unanimous approval. On this matter of sending $35,000,000 out of the country there has been no expression of opinion on the part of the people; they have not had an opportunity of passing judgment on the policy of the present Administration. It may be argued that they passed judgment on the Liberal naval policy at the last election, but it has been repeatedly pointed out that except in the province of Quebec, the naval question was not an issue during the last election. In the other provinces it may have been incidentally referred to, but very little was said about it, and there was no real issue in that regard between the two parties. In the province of Quebec, whilst perhaps there may have been disclosed a sentiment antagonistic to the Liberal naval policy, there was no approval of the policy now enunciated by the Government. They have no mandate from the people, and before embarking upon this policy of sending contributions to the Old Country, or even of sending one contribution, they should obtain the assent and approval of the people. More than that, I say that this policy is fraught with grave oonstitutional dangers. I have here a clipping which expresses the idea I wish to convey betteT than I could possibly express it:
The question is not whether Canada shall accept her national obligations in matters of naval defence. Neither is battleship construction in Britain or in Canada the vital
uestion. All this high sounding talk about
anada's incompetence, indulged in by Mr. Borden and his associates and echoed by Mr. Churchill, gpes wide of the mark. The supreme question is: Shall Canada maintain and control her own sea forces, as she has maintained and controlled her own land forces, or shall she surrender the first right of a free nation and pay defence taxes to a government not elected by the Canadian people and not amendable to Canadian opinion? That question pushes all matters of what and when and how and where into the background. The man who does not see how everything greatly worth while in Canada's national life is involved in such a problem is not equipped for discussing the issue now before Parliament.

What paper is that
from?

I think it is quoted
from the Globe; I di.l not pay much attention to its source, but the sentiment expressed is a noble and patriotic one, and should have a place in the breast of every true Canadian. Does it not sound a great deal like some of the utterances of the men who m days gone by fought for responsible government? I cannot understand how any man from the province of Nova Scotia, where the people, under the leadership of Joseph Howe, fought the great battle for constitutional rights and liberties, for free speech and responsible government, and for the control of their own affairs, as against Downing Street rule; I cannot understand, I say, how any man from the province of Nova Scotia would for a moment stand by this policy of contribution,, Hon. gentlemen say that in voting this $35,000,000 we are not in any way destroying our autonomy or losing any part of our independence. That $35,000,000 goes to the Old Country; we have no control over it after it is converted into battleships. That is the principle which we say is objectionable; that is the principle which the right hon. leader of the Government himself has held as objectionable. He has repeatedly placed himself on record as saying that unless we have a voice in the affairs of the British, Empire, and unless we -have control and direction over the movements of the ships, we should not subscribe to a policy of contribution.

I notice in the
memorandum from the Admiralty read by the Prime Minister on December 5 last, the following words:
The Prime Minister of the Dominion oi Canada has invited His Majesty's Government throngh the Board of Admiralty to prepare a statement of the present and immediately prospective requirements of the naval defence of the Empire for presentation to the Canadian Parliament if the Dominion Cabinet deem it necessary.

My right hon. friend
says ' I did not.' Would he allow me to ask if any member of his Government made any communications ?

And would that answer also apply to the statement made by Mr. Churchill in his communication of the 24th of January as to the impossibility of Canada securing and training sufficient recruits to man one cruiser.
Mr. CARVELL.

speechtext: There was simply inquiry as to the subject matter; the correspondence has been laid before the House.

Then I am to understand that there was no correspondence regarding this matter excepting what has been laid before the House. It perhaps throws some light on the subject, and yet after all it is somewhat remarkable that the British Admiralty would send out to the Canadian people two memorandums of such tremendous importance as those referred to, simply on a verbal conversation between the Prime Minister of Canada and either the First Lord of the Admiralty or some official in his department.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend will not misunderstand me. I did not say I had no conversation on that subject with the First Lord of the Admiralty, and I have no recollection of having a conversation on that particular subject.

My right hon. friend
says there are no communications excepting what have been laid on the table of the House and, if he has no recollection of conversations on the subject, we must assume that the First Lord of the Admiralty has simply gathered this information from newspaper reports, probably from statements made by Conservative orators. Possibly he may have seen it in the London Times. Any way, I am glad to know that the First Lord of the Admiralty had no official right to make such scandalous statements, and what I regard as untrue statements, with respect to the good name of Canada as to her ability to man ships.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I presume that the First Lord of the Admiralty had access to all public documents of this country relating to this matter. I assume that the information came from that source.

That is all I wanted to know. I think by the time we get through with this argument we may find out something about the character of the information that this man Churchill is giving to the world regarding Canada, and the sources from which he obtained his knowledge. I wonder if my right hon. friend realized when he was making his grand stand stage play in this House on the night of the 10th of March last, what would be the consequence of reading a document purporting to come from the First Lord of the British Admiralty based on no better information than Mr. Churchill had when he made that statement. It only shows the part which Mr. Churchill has played in this whole nefarious transaction-and I use that word advisedly and do not think it is too strong to express the real sentiments of the Canadian people after we

come to consider this matter from all standpoints.
We had a little attempt at explanation of the policy of the Government on the part of the Minister of Marine last evening, after a quiescent interval of something like a month. It is most remarkable that he could throw no further light upon the subject than he did. The Government seems to be perfectly willing to sit quiet in their seats and take no part in the debate and give us no further information. Things have happened in the last month and in the last three months and enough things have happened in the last six months to cause a Government which really wanted to work for the best interests of the country to call a halt in this whole thing. As I understand, the Minister of Marine has put up the only argument which the Government intends to or can put up in answer to the criticisms of this proposition made by members on this side of the House. The whole gist of his argument was that because the Pore River Shipbuilding Company ac Quincy, Mass., had made a financial failure, it was impossible to build ships in Canada. There cannot be any other reason for his alluding to that company, [f any hon. gentleman can show any other possible application I would be glad to make way for him.

It seems to me that it was clear to every hon. gentleman in this House that the reason the minister referred to the Fore River -Shipbuilding Company was to prove that the member for St. John did not know what he was talking about in that particular instance.

The Viekers-Maxim
Company do.

They do not, they
build the ships, g.uns and turrets.
Oh, yes, they do.

Even then there are a
hundred other things that they do not build. The Minister of Marine tries to use the unfair, dishonest argument made by Mr. Churchill in his letter-and I again use that word advisedly-to prove that we cannot build ships in Canada because it is necessary to have all these different collateral establishments to build all the materials that enter into the construction and equipment of a battleship. Of course, it is necessary to have guns to go into a ship, but I think I am safe in saying that there is not a ship-building establishment in the United States that manufactures its own guns. In fact, there are only two ship-building plants in the British Empire that manufacture their own guns: the Armstrong, Whitworth Company at Newcastle, and Vickers, Sons & Maxim. They do manufacture their own guns, but all the other ship-building firms buy their guns from whatever concern happens to have them in the market. In the United States the Fore River Shipbuilding Company bought its guns from the Bethlehem Steel Company. I only mention these things to show what an unfair argument the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries attempted to make last evening. He even went so far as to say that if we wanted to build 8 ship in Canada, we would need engine works costing $5,000,000. I do not believe there is a ship-building firm in the world that builds its own engines and boilers.
When my hon. friend from Antigonish (Mr. Chisholm) was speaking I was looking up something about the United States navy, and I found in Burgoyne's Annual
That was a concocted memorandum.
I do not know whether it was or not, but I believe it was. I cannot conceive of a responsible official, such as this gentleman, Commander Roper, on the very day before a general election-

And without being
asked.
Mr. CARVELL-when the policy of constructing ships in Canada was one of the principal policies of the Government then in existence, and the principal policyinthe province of Quebec, leaving a memorandum of that kind without being asked and of his own motion. It simply is not common sense. My hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) was his minister for something like two weeks and during that time he never made reference to it. Yet that is the memorandum which the Minister of Marine and Fisheries states he found in the department.

My hon. friend might
add that a year previously the same Commander Roper expressed a radically different view about the Canadian navy, and for having expressed that view, he was threatened by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) with being brought before the bar of the House.

I remember that incident very distinctly indeed. But even if the incident referred to by my hon. friend from Rouville had never taken place, I repeat there is no responsible official, no man who knows as much as Commander Roper does, who would dare do such a thing, who would ever conceive of doing such a thing. Imagine an official preparing a memorandum the day before the general election condemning the Government on a certain line of policy which was being discussed at the polls! It is not conceivable. The only reasonable supposition is that that he prepared that memorandum afterwards and dated it back. It is due to this House and the people of the country that this man Roper, if he is still in the employ of this Government, should be brought back to Canada, brought before the Bar of the House and compelled to say when he did write it. There is some proof of it somewhere. There is probably a stenographer somewhere around Ottawa who wrote that article, and if we could find him we would know how it was concocted. It was the most ridiculous proposition that I ever heard of since I have been in the House of Commons. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries falls back on a report like that as a justification for refusing to carry out the agreement. Why does he not come out like a man and say that he did not carry out this agreement because the Nationalists of Quebec would not let him do it? Does he suppose that he is fooling anybody in Canada when he tells them this cock-and-bull story? Does he suppose that every man who Teads and thinks does not know why he did not carry out this agreement? Does he not know that his leader issued manifesto after manifesto, in Quebec and in other parts of the country, all condemning the iLaurier naval policy? When my hon. friend came into office, of course, he could not sign the contract. Of course, he could not enter into a policy which he had fought and which the Nationalists had fought in the province of Quebec. He turned it down because he had to. I am almost ashamed that a man representing my own province should come here and put forth the finding of this memorandum as a reason why he did not sign that contract.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman is using strong words.

I do not wish to say
anything that is unparliamentary. I am not saying anything against the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, but I am giv-

ing my own opinion of his action and stating how I feel about it. I want to say something about the obsolescence of these vessels that the Laurier Government were ready to contract for and for which tenders were in the possession of the Naval Department when the present Government came into power. The tenders were to build these ships in St. John. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries may say that my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) stated that if this Government had signed the contract they might have been built on the St. Lawrence. If the Government had signed the contract these vessels might have been built at Montreal, Sydney or Halifax, but let me tell the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries that the tender which he found when he came into office and the deposit of $100,000 which had not been returned were not for building ships in the city of Montreal, but for building ships in the city of St. John, and he knows it. The people of St. John do not care about what might have happened if the Government had gone on and done this, that or some other thing, but the question is: Why did not the Minister of Marine and Fisheries sign that contract and why did he not allow these ships to be built in St. John? That is the question we ask him and that is the question that we are going to continue to ask him. He may say that he has Commander Roper's statement that these ships would be obsolescent before they were completed. I turn again to Burgoyne's Naval Annual, page 345, where reference is made to the type of vessel for which tenders have been called and where Messers. Cammell, Laird & Co., had agreed to construct in St. John for, I think, $1,900,000.
Carried.
Oh, do not measure them in your own bushel.
I do not think my hon. friend from Halton is getting very much of the loaves and fishes now, and he may be a little sore when loaves and fishes are mentioned.
There is no occasion for me to be.
If the hon. gentleman were looking for a good fat contract, he might be more successful in landing it than he is in landing the higher office at which he aims. I sympathize with the hon. gentleman.

Thank you very
kindly.

If there is a man on the other side of the House with whom I do really sympathize, it is the hon. member for Halton, and I am sorry that my reference to loaves and fishes ruffled his usually smooth temper.
Oh, not at all.

I do not think there is much chance of the Government losing the Nationalists, but if they are going to hold them they must not build ships in Canada; they must not recruit men in Canada, and they must dismiss the men who already have been recruited in Canada. That is the one condition of the support of the Nationalists, and so long as the Prime Minister complies with that condition, he will have their loyal support. At all events, that is the reason the Minister of Marine did not sign the contract to build the vessels at St. John and not because the vessels would be obsolescent before they were completed.
When the Prime Minister introduced this measure on the 5th day of December last, he proposed it on the sole ground that a condition of emergency existed in the
British Empire, and that if this contribution were not made the British Empire might go to pieces. True, the Prime Minister did not put it in as plain English as I do now, but that wa3 the substance of what he said. And, if my right hon. friend omitted anything in that direction, it was supplied by his followers who were allowed to speak during the first fortnight of the debate. One after the other of them got up and delivered himself of the German scare as the sole argument for sending this $35,000,000 out of the country. It may be well to call attention to the language used by the Prime Minister on that memorable occasion, the 5th of December, and it will be found that the only reason he gave for this proposal was directed to the fear that some fine day the German navy might descend upon the British Isles. He read it with the greatest satisfaction, and it was applauded to the echo by his followers. In this statement he practically set forth that there was an emergency. Let me read it to the House again:
It may be fairly asked what we would do if we were in power to-day with regard to a great question of this kind. It seems to me that our plain course and duty would be this: The Government of this country are able to ascertain and to know, if they take the proper action for that purpose, whether the conditions which face the Empire at this time in respect of naval defence are grave. If we were in power we would endeavour to find that out, to get a plain, unvarnished answer to that question, and if the answer to that question, based upon the assurance of the Government of the Mother Country and the report of the naval experts of the Admiralty were such-and I think it would be such- as to demand instant and effective action by this country, then I would appeal to Parliament for immediate and effective aid, and if Parliament did not give immediate and effective aid I would appeal from Parliament to the people of the. country.
Any reasonable man must take that to mean that he went to England and found that a real condition of emergency existed, a condition which required immediate and effective aid. If there was any question as to his intention or the grounds upon which he was applying to Parliament, his succeeding remarks dispelled any doubt as to that. They are as follows:
Then, Sir, as to the permanent policy, I think the people have a right to be consulted. I do not know whether I have made my position clear but I have done so according to my humble capacity. I think the question of Canada's co-operation upon a permanent basis in Imperial defence involves very large and wide considerations.
That was his belief as to the condition of affairs in December, 1912. He asked Parliament to grant $35,000,000 on the ground that a real emergency existed at that time. After this money was granted,

he intended to take up the question of a permanent policy. I want to be fair to him. I want at least to be logical in any conclusion that I may draw from the facts that I am giving to the House. I wonder if my right hon. friend could find any man on the other side of the House who would argue that a condition of emergency exists to-day. Even the Montreal Star has given up that idea. About six weeks ago when people were getting away from the crux of the question, that paper came out with an editorial, in which it said: They are forgetting the emergency. Why, the Montreal Star has forgotten it now. No reasonable thinking man in the British Empire would say that there is an emergency at the present time. My right hon. friend in his address of the 5th of December, made the air lurid in his description of the condition of affairs existing in the North sea. He told us how many vessels the Germans had in the North sea.,	a.nd
how many the British had in the North sea. We heard the thunder roll and saw the lightning flash. The battle of Armageddon was at hand, and the German navy was ready to come over and to blow us up at any moment. Many things have happened since that time. When my right hon. friend made his .speech in December, 1912, a condition of affairs existed in Europe which made it very easy for him to make an argument even though it was not based on facts. There was a war between Turkey and the Balkans which threatened to set Europe on fire. Turkey was humiliated and practically driven out of Europe, and finally bad to come to the Powers and say:	We plaee_ ourselves entirely in your hands; do with us as you think best and we will be satisfied.
Then my friends got hope from another complication in Europe. The Montenegrins captured the fortress of Scutari and said that they were going to hold it. Every hon. member knows that Austria determined that Montenegro should not be permitted to hold Scutari, but that Scutari should become Austrian or Albanian. It looked as if there was going to be war over that. Every paper came out with scare headlines; but Scutari has now been abandoned by the Montenegrins, and Europe is at peace and at rest as it has not been for the last forty years. The German Empire for the last ten years has been spending enormous sums on its navy. It has transferred its energies now to its army. It is increasing its army on a peace footing by about 250,000 men; and, in order to get the necessary funds, it has been compelled to resort to what ' I might call the expropriation of public property. It has had to assess a tax upon the property of the people which amounts almost to confiscation. France Mr. CARVBLL.
has increased her land forces by lengthening the term of service from two to three years. A new force has arisen in the Balkans. A million armed men are there who are supposed to be the allies of Russia. The whole theatre of trouble in Europe has been transferred from the water to the land. So far as any person who thinks and reads can see, it will be generations before there will be any question of trouble on the ocean. If any trouble takes place in Europe in the future, it must be on the land. The German Empire, without any question whatever, has agreed to the proposition of restricting its construction of war vessels to the ratio of ten German vessels to sixteen British. With an agreement like that, why should we go into this un-Canadian- and I might say unpatriotic proposition to send this money out of the country and to establish a condition of affairs which sooner or later must be broken by the people of Canada, and which cannot be broken without causing trouble either here or in the Mother Country?
These are matters which I think my right hon. friend would do well to consider carefully before he attempts to force this matter through by closure, as we understand he intends doing. I think he will have some difficulty in getting it through in any other way. I am not making a threat; I am only stating a fact. If we were justified in December, 1912, in refusing to agree to this un-Canadian proposition, we are a hundred times more justified in refusing to agree to it now, when the very reason put forward by my right hon. friend for its existence has absolutely failed and has ceased to exist. I do not wonder that he does not attempt to justify this proposition at this stage of the debate. I do not wonder that he has left the matter to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, who has tried to draw the attention of the people away from the fact that we can build ships in Canada, by stating that a shipbuilding firm in the United States has got into financial difficulties and has been sold out to a larger firm. That will not put it out of existence but will enable it to continue on a wider basis than in the past. I do not wonder that my right hon. friend will not allow any of his followers to make a speech or to endeavour to justify this proposition. I do not wonder that none of his newspaper followers in Canada have attempted to do such a thing. The reading public are reasonable beings. They are able to read the signs of the times, just the same as hon. members on this side of the House are. They know that condition of emergency has ceased to exist. They know that the idea of forcing this Bill through is taken up only because the Government are compelled to do so at the be-

best of their Nationalist followers, and not because it is necessary for Canada or for the British Empire.
Even at this late date, I consider that the right hon. the Prime Minister would not lose in prestige; that he would gain in prestige; that he would be stamped as a man of big proportions if he would have the manhood to say:	Conditions have
changed since I introduced this Bill in 1912. The condition of emergency which I thought existed then has ceased to exist. There is no danger of trouble arising in Great Britain. An agreement has been entered into between Great Britain and Germany by which naval construction shall be limited in the ratio of sixteen to ten. He can give all these reasons without any loss of prestige, and, indeed, I think he would gain a great deal of prestige if he were to stand up and say: The conditions have changed; therefore I will withdraw this Bill. If he would do that, there would be no trouble about agreeing on a policy which would be of great benefit to Canada as a whole.
My hon. friend has said that, although we are now giving this money, we are going to have a permanent policy. My impression is that we have the permanent policy before us now. In introducing this Bill, my hon. friend said that the Canadian ships were to be stationed in the North sea, and he and those of his followers whom he allowed to speak during the first two or three weeks of this debate placed great emphasis upon the conditions in the North sea. They wanted the ships to be in the firing line when Armageddon comes; they wanted to be represented not by their men, who would be of some use, but by their money; they wanted to be where there would be no danger that the sons of Canada would be disembowelled by German bullets. When it was suggested by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House that, if we had a fleet unit on the Atlantic, that fleet unit could get to the North sea in six days, we were told that the whole danger would have passed over before the fleet could get there. That argument was made use of up to March 10, when my right hon. friend read this remarkable production from the Right Hon. Winston Churchill. My right hon. friend hesitated long and anxiously before producing that letter; I do not wonder that he did so. I am surprised that a responsible minister of the_ Crown in Britain should write a letter which contains an insult to one-half the Canadian people and a libel upon the other half-an insult when he SR,ys that the people of Canada have not the brains, the pluck, the energy and the ability to do what other countries have done, and a libel upon our workmen fn Canada when ' 293
he says that there cannot be found in this country men to drive rivets, build cranes or man shipyards. He even intimated that we had no soil in Canada sufficiently solid to support the ways for holding a ship. As I say, I do not wonder that my right hon. friend hesitated long and anxiously before he presented that memorandum to Parliament. I do not wonder that when it was read in this House it created a storm that my right hon. friend did not anticipate; I do not wonder that it created a tempest not only in Parliament but throughout the country. I do not wonder that his own party papers, as well as the Liberal press, condemned him and his party for repeating that libel upon the Canadian people. But the storm created in Canada was but a gentle zephyr compared with the storm that took place in Great Britain when this matter became known. It is well known that in Britain, not only the Conservative press but the Liberal papers supporting the Hon. Mr. Churchill, condemned him in the severest possible manner for his action. An hon.mem-ber of the British Parliament gave notice of a resolution of censure upon the Admiralty for writing such a letter and for offering such an insult to the labouring people of the Dominion of Canada, and it was only on account of the exigencies of British polities that this gentleman was not allowed to make his motion of censure. It is well known in England that if the members of the British Parliament were given a chance to tell Mr. Churchill -what they thought of him, he would be driven out of the Government, and, as in this event such great reforms as Home Rule, the abolition of plural voting, and other great social reforms now being projected in England might go to the wall, for their own self-preservation the Liberal party in Britain abstained from giving this gentleman an opportunity of placing upon the First Lord of the Admiralty that censure which the parliamentarians of Britain would like to mete out to him for offering this insult to Canada. Then Mr. Churchill had to do something to pacify public opinion in Britain, and the naval emergency was shifted from the North sea to Gibraltar; the Canadian ships were linked up with the Sultan of Perak and the Malay States. At first the Right Hon. Winston Churchill would have us believe that the Canadian ships in Shis flying squadron were to be associated with those of Australia and New Zealand. But Australia said two or three years ago: We will have .none of your flfying squadron; we are looking after our own affairs, building our cwn navy, manning and owning it, and if the time comes when the British Empire is in need of aid we shall place the ships



at the disposal of the British Admiralty. It is true that New Zealand had adopted a policy of contribution, and that she handed one ship over to the British Empire. But even New Zealand has gene back on that policy, and, if we correctly interpret the remarks of Colonel Allen, who was in this country last week, it is evident that New Zealand will have nothing more to do with contributions, and intends to pursue the manly course of building her own ships, manning and .maintaining them, 'and, like Australia, placing them at the disposal of the British Admiralty when the hour of danger should arise. That is the course Canada Should adopt. When Winston Churchill -trans-Jeired these vessels to Gibraltar, while he may have pleased some people in Britain, he did not please my right hon. friend, ike Conservative party in Canada saw that the whole argument they had been putting up to the people of Canada was by this course swept away. For two months subsequent to December 5, 1912, they tried to make the people of Canada believe that the vessels must be in the North sea when Armageddon comes, to fight the Germans, but Winston Churchill now says: We do not want those vessels in the North sea; we have the ships and the men and the money and the resources, and we can take care of ourselves; we are going to send these Canadian vessels to Gibraltar. Then my hon. friends opposite saw that their argument was entirely shattered, and, while I have no actual knowledge of the matter, I can quite conceive of the wires being kept red-hot with cablegrams going across to Churchill from my right hon. friend saying: Look at the hole you have put me in. Then Mr. Churchill says:	I must
placate my friends in Canada. It is true we can take care of ourselves in the North *sea; it is true that we have made arrangements with Germany by which future naval construction will be reduced to the ratio of 16 to 10; it is true that we do not want the Canadian warships in the North sea, and it is equally true we have not got the men to man them even if they were there.
The hon. gentleman has spoken very glowingly of Australia. Is it true or not true that Australia considers its navy a component part of the navy of the Empire ?
It is both true and not true.
That is just what I expected.

It is true in time of trouble, it is not true in time of peace, and if any man can conceive any better Canadian doctrine than that I would like Mir. CARVELL.
to hear him speak now or forever hold his peace.
. Mr. BURNHAM:	It is independent,
that is what it is.

My hon. friend must
not get excited over independence, we will discuss that later, and I hope my hon. friend will be permitted to make a speech on that subject. My right hon. friend ought to see that there are dozens of his followers anxious to give the public their views on this question. Free speech never hurt any country or any party. Every time one of my hon. friends opposite asks a question it is an illustration of this great doctrine of free speech and of the danger attending the method of burking free speech which has been adopted by this Government. The Australian fleet, I be-live the moment there is a possibility of danger to the British Empire, will be placed unreservedly under the British Admiralty.
