I will tell my hon. friend what will happen, so far as I am concerned. So far as I am concerned the Canadian navy will be at the disposal ^of the British Admiralty the moment the time of emergency comes or it Is required for the defence of the Empire, and if my right hon. friend has any doubt about that let him move an amendment to section 22 and 23 of the Canadian Naval Service Act in order to improve it in this respect; then he will see if every man on this side of the House will not vote for him. My right hon. friend dare not amend the Canadian Naval Service Act in that way. He is the greatest sinner of them all in this regard, because when speaking on this question at one time he harked back to an answer given by the right hon. leader of the Opposition to a supposed question when the Naval Service Act was under consideration by the Committee of the Whole House. He stated a certain condition of affairs and asked the -right hon. gentleman what would happen under those conditions under the Canadian Naval Service Act, and the right hon. leader of the Opposition gave the only logical answer which could he given, the

logical answer that any hon. gentleman would give, and which I for one would never for a moment go back on. If my right hon. friend fears that some action might be taken by a future Canadian Government that should not be taken, because of the wording of sections 22 and 23 of the Canadian Naval Service Act, and these are the only ones referring to it, I say to him:	Amend the Act and put it
exactly in the same form as the Australian and New Zealand Act and he will not hear a word of dissent from this side of the House. If that were done we would have a Canadian navy controlled by the Dominion Government in time of peace and at the service of the Empire in time of war.

Is my hon. friend
of the same mind as the right hon. leader of the Opposition, who said that if circumstances arose again the same as those existing at the time of the Crimean war he would not send the Canadian navy to the assistance of Great Britain?

I was not on this earth at the time of the Crimean war, neither was my hon. friend; and, while I know something about the history of that war,
I do not care what would have happened in 1854; what I am talking about is what is happening in 1913 and what will happen m the future and I am telling my hon. friend what would be my attitude in case a Canadian navy were built and certain conditions arose. Under the Canadian Naval Service Act there is not a word line or expression which prevents the Canadian Government from doing anything they have a mind to; they may send the Canadian navy to the British Admiralty any day they want to, or they may send them to the Crimea or anywhere else, the only condition is that if they transfer it to the British Admiralty they must call Parliament together within ten or fifteen days to provide funds. They must do the same with regard to the navy as with regard to the militia. The Militia Act, passed a few years after Confederation, provides that if you send the militia of Canada out of the country you must call Parliament together to provide funds. The same thing applies to the navy. The Militia Act provides that the militia must be controlled by the Canadian Government and by nobody else; but if the militia be handed over to the British Government a new condition of affairs arises and Parliament must be called together. If my right hon. friend or any of his followers have any doubt about that let the Prime Minister bring down an amendment to the Canadian Naval Service Act which will eliminate the boggy which they profess to see in those two clauses or any other clauses.
293*
And you will vote against it.

And I will vote for it. My right hon. friend dare not bring in such an amendment, his Nationalist allies will not allow it. I think he is having enough trouble with the Nationalist wing of his party now without attempting to amend the Naval Service Act. One minister of the Crown said last year that they would abolish the Canadian Naval Service Act. The Prime Minister seems to have kept them quiet by arguments or promises, promises I presume, and they have remained quiet and have allowed this session to go on without demanding the repeal of the Naval Service Act. It is true that they have not all voted with the Government on all occasions, but enough of them have voted with the Government to keep them in power and I presume that the Government will be able to get through the session without repealing the Naval Service Act. But if they have any doubt about this side of the House or any doubt about the efficiency of the Canadian Naval Service Act and want to make it plainer that the Canadian navy will automatically pass into the hands of the Admiralty in time of war, all they have to do is to change the wording of the Act and they will not find any necessity of applying closure to pass such a measure through the House.
At six o'clock, House resumed, and then took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock, and again went into Committee. (Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair.)

Before six o'clock I was discussing as briefly as possible the objections which my hon. friends opposite profess to have to the Canadian Naval Service Act, and in order that I may leave no doubt whatever as to my meaning in that respect, I wish to call the attention of the committee to those sections of the Canadian Naval Service Act which seems to have been a stumbling block to my hon. friends opposite. We did not hear much about this Act in the province of New Brunswick in the last campaign, and very little I think in the maritime provinces.
We heard something about it in Quebec.

Yes, but in Quebec they did not find the same fault with it as they did in the province of Ontario. In Quebec they found fault because it was doing something for Great Britain, but in Ontario the fault they found was that it did nothing for the Empire. They called it a separatist navy because they claimed that under the

Canadian Naval Service Act the Canadian Government would not be compelled to do anything for the Empire in case of need.
I wish to show how easy it would be for my hon. friends opposite to adopt this law and to make it mean anything they desired. They can make all the changes they like, though, according to my judgment, no changes are necessary, because as I consider it, the law gives the Government all the power which they need to protect Canada and to assist in the protection of the Empire. To my mind we want no better law than the one we have at present, despite what the Minister of Marine and Fisheries may say. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has not been able to implement the promise he made to his Nationalist friends a year ago. We know that a little more than a year ago there were grave doubts as to whether his Nationalist allies would not desert the Conservative party in a body, with the result that my hon. friend was compelled to make a promise that the Government would repeal the Canadian Naval Service Act. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has not carried out that promise yet. The only sections in this Act which seems to bother my hon. friend and especially Imperialists like my hon. friend from Peterborough (Mr. Burnham), are sections 22 and 23, and in order that we may know definitely what these are I wish to place them on 'Hansard.' Section 22 reads:
The Governor in Council may place the naval forces or any part thereof, on active service at any time when its appears advisable so to do by reason of an emergency.
Section 23 reads:
In case of an emergency the Governor in Council, may place at the disposal of His Majesty, for general service in the Royal navy, the naval service or any part thereof, any ships or vessels of the naval service, and the officers and seamen serving in such ships or vessels, or any officers or seamen belonging to the naval service.
In order to know what is meant by an emergency, you can refer back to section 2, the interpretation clause, and you have the following in sub-section (d):
Emergency means war, invasion or insurrection real or apprehended.
Therefore if there is war, invasion, or insurrection, either real or pretended the Government would have the right, as the law now stands, to place the whole Canadian naval service under the control of the British Admiralty, to do with it whatever they had a mind to. My hon. friends say that it is a separatist Bill, and they have wasted months and months of time, and I am going to say tons and tons of literature, in trying to prove that this is a disloyal measure. Having read all the Mr. CARVELL.
clauses bearing on that branch of the case, I repeat that if my right hon. friend thinks that this is not a proper Act, he now has control of this Parliament, and all he has to'do is to bring down any amending clause he might think necessary, and if the Canadian Naval Service Act in the future is not what it ought to be, the burden is on him. I hope we will hear nothing more from hon. gentlemen opposite, or from their press, about a separatist navy or about a Naval Service Act which will not allow the ships of Canada to go to the defence of the Empire in case of an emergency.
That is surely not the point.

Government who have had the courage to open their mouths upon this question-that these vessels are to remain permanently with the British Admiralty and that if they are to remain permanently with the British Admiralty there will be no Canadian navy.
That is the position of one branch of the Conservative party in Canada; that is the real meaning of the policy of the Imperialist branch. That is the real agreement that was made in London last summer between the right hon. Prime Minister and his colleagues and the British Admiralty. This agreement was not even put in writing according to the confession of my hon. friend this afternoon. It is an agreement that was made verbally. This is the agreement that these hon. gentlemen made when they told Mr. Churchill that we could not get recruits or seamen in Canada, that we could not build ships, that we were a nation of do nothings, hewers of wood and drawers of water, that we cannot do anything but pay, pay, pay. I give my right hon. friend credit at least that he did not put this agreement in writing. It will not come up in judgment against him in the form of a letter because he had judgment enough not to put it on paper.
Now, I come down to the other branch of the Conservative party and let us see what they say about this question. The Conservative party in Canada is a conglomeration of Imperialism and Nationalism. I have dealt with the Imperialist side of the question and now I come to the National side. I have here an extract from a paper published in the province of Quebe'c which is, I understand, the principal organ of the Nationalist party in that province. It is not Le Devoir, because I think Le Devoir is now out of harmony with the leaders of the Nationalist Conservative party in Quebec. It is La Se-maine which, in English, I understand, means The Week. I have here a translation which, I am assured, is an accurate one, of an article published in that paper, and I am so much convinced of the accuracy of the translation that I am willing to read it, place it on ' Hansard,' and allow any hon. gentlemen opposite, who desire to do so, to discuss it. This, I am also told, is the personal organ of the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Blondin), a gentleman who occupies a very important position in this House and in the Conservative party of Canada. I might go farther than that and say it is not only his personal organ but it is really his production. I have here some real jewels of thought, showing what the Nationalists are preaching before the people, and what they say this policy means:
Grand Mfere, Champlain county, Friday, May 2nd

Mr. CARVELL.
This is not ancient history; it is only last Friday.
Last Scruples-Opposition to a Moral Aid has no Sense-Neither has a Referendum.
In Opposition said the other day an exminister,-* One must play the part of comedians.' Evidently this is the role of the present Opposition, as that of the critic to always find fault, to always find awful and terrible and bad with the present Government. It is the duty of the latter to defend itself, and of the public to judge without losing its senses on the furore or the simulated fears of the constitutional enemies of the Cabinet. The idea of a Canadian navy, the phantom of periodical contributions, the assailants who might prey on our cheese and butter on the high seas, as well as the famous so-called gift of thirty-five millions, are so many ruses made up for the fight, but documents, reasons and common sense have already triumphed over them all. It has now been admitted even by the Opposition, that the Borden proposals mean none of these. They amount purely and simply to a demonstration of friendship which cannot take, until many years, any other form but that of moral aid; at least as long as the people will not have been consulted.
There remains another last scruple which we must dispel. The Borden contribution was formerly declared by the Quebec Conservatives to be no less nefarious than the Laurier navy. One must not forget that that contribution meant the immediate gift of a sum of money from hand to hand to the Admiralty. It was a gift pure and simple. The present Bill mentions no gift; it provides for the construction in two or three years' time of three Canadian vessels which may be loaned to England in five or six years' time.
Not very much emergency in that.
It bears no resemblance whatsoever to the Borden proposal when made by him in opposition. There is no more talk of contribution, and this Bill only lends a moral help to England, and safeguards the rights of the Canadian people. Therefore, it does not justify by one single iota this last scruple.
Moreover, it is certain that it would be foolish in the present bitter political turmoil at home, and in face of the European crisis, where whole empires are at stake, to attempt to settle by a referendum a question of moral aid. This referendum would suppose that the people at large, and above all, those who take especial interest in international events, are familiar with this question, which from day to day, from hour to hour, changes its aspect, becomes acute with the fall of Adrianople, is appeased by the Bulgarian peace, and is revived with the aerial incidents on the frontiers and with the siege of Scutari. In the midst of so many menacing snags the crew must not fight around the rudder. The parliament is elected; a majority is formed; to that majority belongs the duty to pilot the ship during the allotted time. Euless anarchy, impoteney and folly are rampant, the people must give the hand to which it has confided its destinies free scope. We are convinced that sooner or later reason shall triumph. As between a premature, if not useless, Canadian navy and a passive contri-

tuition without any condition, the Conservative .party has selected the most happy solution,-a loan which gives a moral aid in the eyes of the world, and which in the last resort reserves to the people the supreme decision The last scruples are therefore wiped out; they will not hinder us from taking the right course.
There is the policy of the Nationalists, but that is mild compared with some of the Test of it. Then there is in great big type on the third page in the same issue of La Semaine on Friday, May 2, the following signed by R. L. Borden:
It has been said that the present policy of the Government was one of an annual and' permanent contribution. TJpon my responsibility of member of the Government 1 deny that absolutely Canada is and shall be the sole master of its destinies.
Next we have the statement of P. E. Blondin, Deputy Speaker, appearing on the same page and following Mr. Borden's declaration. This is it:
To accept the Opposition compromise, the Laurier navy added to the loan of three dreadnoughts would have meant the ruin of the Nationalist policy, of which Mr. Borden has respected the principles in his Bill.
P. E. Blondin, Deputy Speaker.

Who is that statement
signed by?

P. E. Blondin, the
Deputy Speaker.
Read it again please?

Here it is:
To accept the Opposition compromise, the Laurier navy added to the loan of three< dreadnoughts would have meant the ruin of .the Nationalist policy, of which Mr. Borden has respected the principles in his Bill.
P. E. Blondin, Deputy Speaker.
I had always supposed that the national policy meant that we should manufacture as much in Canada as we could; but here we are sending $35,000,000 out of the country to build ships in England, and we are going to deprive Canadians of all classes of the right to participate in the expenditure of that money. On April 24, La Semaine publishes the following:
Important Words.
To a group of leading Conservatives of the district of Three Rivers, Mr. Blondin, M.P., for Champlain, made the other day the following declaration, which our friends will read with pleasure, and keep in their memory :-	,
The march of events confirms more and more that the moral effect of a demonstration is the primordial object of both the British and Canadian Governments. Now that the Liberals, feeling that they are defeated, do not care to agitate public opinion with the
phantom of a permanent contribution, they themselves admit that the Borden Bill 'has no other .meaning but that of the moral effect of an offer. The moral effect is immediate, but the oiler cannot be put into execution only later on. The clear mind of the Prime Minister has found the solution, the most diplomatic and the most practical,_ in so far as it satisfies all possible opinions in England and over here, namely, satisfactory to the people of Canada which without party distinction desires to do something,-some by-way of contribution, others by way of beginning of a local navy. It frames a measure whioh first, gives something,-if a moral aid is something, -second, which does not prevent any other solution once the people shall have decided, and third, it is a measure which binds us to nothing definitely.
The moral effect is not spoiled by party divisions in the Canadian Parliament, because such divisions do not arise from the faot that any of the two parties refuse to help England; and to those who, like Mr. iBourassa, are not willing to do anything, this measure gives to be understood that nothing will be done until two or three years; that is to say, before a general election.
Now, Mr. Chairman (Mr. Blondin), you will appreciate the last remarks I have read from La Semaine, and I hope the Prime Minister will appreciate them in the same manner. It all goes to show the fearful humbug this proposition is. In order to humbug the people of Canada, five months ago they were told by the Prime Minister there was a fearful emergency and that we must send this $35,000,000 to save the Empire, and here we are told by the Nationalist wing of the Conservative party that the thing does not mean anything at all; that we can have the vessels built in two or three years for moral effect, and that it is only done to satisfy public opinion and that it will not amount to anything. Is that the position the great Conservative party of Canada should take on a matter of such imperial importance?
Certainly not.
I am delighted to find a responsive chord in the heart of hon. member for Hamilton.

I say the Conservative
party never would act in such a dastardly way.

My hon. friend from
Hamilton did not know of this before, and I am glad to be able to give him some of the inside history of his own party.
The trouble is that you did not.

I have been telling him all along that he was led by the nose by the Nationalists and he did not believe it. I say that the Nationalist wing of the Conservative party are the men who are doing the leading; they are the men who

are directing the policy of the party, and they have good reason to smile and be gracious. It is no wonder the Nationalists are happy; they are making the Government do what they want them to do. But what have the Imperialists of Toronto got to say about it? I do not wonder the hon. member for Hamilton gets hot under the collar when he hears this; I do not wonder he feels insulted when he is told what is going on. My friends opposite are trying to play the same game they played two years ago; they are attempting to preach one thing in Ontario and another thing in Quebec. The moment there is a suspicion of a by-election in London you find the same crew going up there with the same weapons and holding the same kind of meetings, and even advertising Protestant meetings. You do not find them advertising Protestant meetings in the province of Quebec. They are playing the same doublehanded game they played two years ago. They are circulating other documents, copies of which have been placed in the hands of I suppose every member in the House, and reference to which was made in the Senate. But that will not succeed for there is an old saying that lightning will not strike twice in the same place.
It struck once anyway.

It struck once at Peterborough. My hon. friend from Peterborough was honest enough to own up to it. The result has been that my friend from Peterborough has never had the gag taken off his mouth since. They have never allowed him to make another speech after his first one.

What about your nine
majority:

This evidently does not suit my hon. friends opposite. I may say that it was not my object in bringing it up that it should suit them. My object was to show them some of the things that are going on in their own party, and incidentally I may show some of the people in the country who vote for them what is going on.
This is the tenth time you have told us that.

Another man who would like to have the gag removed from his mouth. I know it hurts my hon. friend from the Sault. I appeal to my right hon. friend to remove the gag from their mouths; otherwise they will explode. He should give them a chance to relieve themselves.
I have tried to show the game which my hon. friends have been playing. I am trying to show the policy which they are preaching in different parts of the country. In my judgment there is only one policy which they are really preaching, and that Mr. CARVELL
is a policy of contribution. There cannot be any other policy than contribution owing to the alliance existing between them and the Nationalist party in Quebec. They want to make a contribution of $35,000,000 this year. Perhaps it will be more than that, because the Minister of Marine and Fisheries admitted that these vessels would cost $39,000,000. Probably by the time you get through, it will be $40,000,000. By the time you run a couple of elections out of it, it will be $50,000,000.
An hon. MEMBER. You ought to know.

That is the point we object to more than anything else. That is what the amendment of my hon. friend from Welland is aimed at. That is the point that is most unconstitutional of all. Every member on this side of the House objects, and I am satisfied that the people of this country will object, when they know that this Government is undertaking to spend $35,000,000 or $40,000,000 of the public money when the people of this country do not know where it is going. My friends are trying to undo the law of responsible government. They are trying to go back to the condition of affairs which existed before responsible government. My friends are trying to put themselves in the position of taking $35,000,000 or $40,000,000 of the public money, of going to England and making a contract of any kind with whomsoever they have a mind to make one, with firms over which we have no control. They wi.-m to expend the money in such' a way that we can have no accounting and that we shall simply receive receipts for it. So far as I am concerned-and 1 think I am expressing the views of many members on this side of the House-I think no government should be entrusted with the right to spend $35,000,000 of our money, unless Parliament has some control over it.
It is true that the Government intend to build three dreadnoughts. When my right hon. friend introduced this Bill on the 5th of December, he told us that these vessels would cost a little better than $11,000,000 apiece. According to the confession of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, they will cost $13,000,000 apiece. He will have them costing $14,000,000 before very long, because the Minister of Marine and Fisheries said last night that the latest American vessels are costing sixteen, seventeen or eighteen million dollars. The Government will be at liberty, if they so choose, to go to England and to make a contract for these vessels for $15,000,000 apiece, and Parliament will not have a word to say about it. They do not even have to call for tenders. They do not have to submit those tenders to Parliament. It is the most serious attack on the

policy of responsible government which has been made since Confederation. The Highways' Bill is only a trifle compared with it and I think that is bad enough. It seems that the whole object of the legislation of this Government is not to help the country but to get control of enormous sums of money to be spent by Order in Council and not by Parliament; to get the right to handle the money entirely without the authority of the representatives of the people and without accounting to the people for its expenditure. That is what we object to, and that is the reason for the amendment moved by my hon. friend from Welland (Mr. German). We are opposing this Bill more upon that point than upon the fact that the money is to be spent out of the country.
If the right hon. the Premier will say that the Government will call foT tenders, that they will take the lowest tender; that they will consult Parliament before the contract is let, it will take away a lot of the sting. They will not do that. They want the whole $35,000,000 in a lump sum. They want to make any contract that they desire to make. If they got this right, I think I can safely say that my friend the Minister of Public Works would finance one election out of it and perhaps he would finance two. I hope the amendment moved by my hon. friend from Welland will be accepted. We have other objections to Taise and other amendments to move to this Bill before it gets through; but that is the cardinal sin in the whole transaction. Behind that is the great question of policy of whether this country is to go on with a policy of contribution, by which we shall send out of this country year after year millions of dollars over which we shall have no control and for which we shall get no benefit, or whether we are to go into a reasonable, sane naval policy of constructing these vessels at home. Let us profit by the experience of the people of Australia and New Zealand who have been at it longer than we have. Let us take the advice of men who have tried both ways. Let us take the advice of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster). Some of us wondered why the Minister of Trade and Commerce was sent out of the country. We are commencing to see the reason. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is of exactly the same opinion to-day that he was in 1909. He was sincere in 1909; he believed in a Canadian navy. He believes in it to-day. He is now in Australia and perhaps he does not realize that conditions have changed here. I find in the Manitoba Free Press of May 3, a despatch from Melbourne, in which the hon. the minister of Trade and Commerce says:
I congratulate Australia on her defence policy; she has set a grand lesson to Canada.
What do you think of that? What better evidence than that of what the policy of Canada ought to be? Australia, who in 1902 entered into a policy of contribution, who made an agreement with the British Government that for ten years she would contribute a million dollars annually, who carried out that agreement, after five years found that it was contrary to the best interests of the country. In 1907 or 1908 she gave notice to the British Government that she would not carry it out any longer than ten years. In 1909 representatives of Australia came to the Imperial conference and said: We have done with contribution; it does not appeal to the best interests of , our people; it does not put us in a position to defend ourselves in case of emergency or trouble; it is un-Australian and un-British. Australia gave notice that she was going to build her own fleet unit. That fleet unit has been built. The first vessels were built in England and the rest in Australia. Their guns are being built in Australia. Every part of those vessels that can be built in Australia is being built there. The Australians are manning those vessels; they are paying for them and if necessary, they will fight in them themselves. That is the policy of Australia; that is the policy which New Zealand is going to adopt, and that is the policy of which the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce said:
I congratulate Australia upon her defence policy. She is setting a grand lesson to Canada.
I hope the right hon. Prime Minister of this country will take these words to 1 heart. I hope he will come to the conclusion that what is good for New Zealand and Australia is good for Canada. I hope he will profit by the experience of our sister colonies. I hope he will not break faith with Australia in the contract made at the Imperial conference of 1909, by which Australia agreed to build a fleet unit on the Pacific, and by which Canada agreed to build certain cruisers and place them on the Pacific and to commence the construction and development of our fleet units. I hope he will take the advice the Minister of Trade and Commerce has given him, and that he will withdraw this Bill. If hon. gentlemen opposite want to change the Naval Service Act in any way, let them do so, but let them proceed with the true Canadian policy of building these vessels in Canada, so far as possible, manning them in Canada, paying for them like men, and be in a position, should occasion arise, to defend Canada's shores, and not hire others to defend them for us.

Moreover, Commander Roper has expressed views totally different from those contained in the memorandum quoted by the hon. minister of Marine and Fisheries. My hon. friend was not a member of the House of Commons during the last Parliament. As we learned last night from my deskmate, the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugs-ley), the hon. gentleman was defeated in 1896, and the House and the country lost his services during the succeeding 'interval. If the hon. gentleman had been a member of this House during the session of 1910 he would have heard his former colleague, who was then the member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), traduce Commander Roper before this House and condemn him because, forsooth, in a speech delivered at the Ottawa Central Exhibition, and in an address delivered before the Canadian Club in this city, he had extolled the policy of the Laurier Government of establishing a navy to be built in Canada, equipped in Canada, maintained by Canadians and controlled by the Dominion Government. My hon. friend is not aware of that; yet he has only to look at Hansard' of the session of 1910, in which he will find the words of Commander Roper. The committee will, I hope, bear with me if I quote just a few sentences. On the 7th of December, 1910, Mr. Monk, then the member for Jacques Cartier, formerly Minister of Public Works, traduced Commander Roper and condemned him most severely for having dared to deliver an address before the Canadian Club, in which he said:
He deprecated the use of the term ' tin-pot ' as applied to the navy, adding: tin-pot
Certainly, they are being denounced by the honest Mr. Bourassa.
Oh, oh.

Mr. Bourassa is no
friend of mine. He has never spared me, and I have never spared him, but I am free to say that he is honest in his convictions. What he preached and what he wrote during the elections of 1911 he stands by to-day; but my hon. friends who preached and wrote as Mr. Bourassa did in 1911 are to-day going against their previous opinions.
What did I say in the elections of 1911?

Speaking from memory- and the words are very vivid in my memory when the hon. gentleman went into the election of Drummond and Arthabaska, he addressed a meeting one Sunday-he desecrated the Sunday by his words. He said to the people of Drummond and Arthabaska: Gentlemen, Sir Wilfrid Laurier starts a navy; he says that it is your navy; he calls it a Canadian navy; but by the Bill the navy belongs to the King; and, said my non. friend, folding his arms, " where is the King of Canada? to what Majesty does Sir Wilfrid reier? " ' That was the language

used by my hon. friend; and if he will refer to Mr. Castell Hopkins' Annual Digest, for 1911, he will find his exact words.

During the election of Drummond-Arthabaska my hon. friend was in South Africa, but I was in Drummond and Arthabasca. All the reports published by Mr. Hopkins and by some Ontario Liberal papers were prepared in Drummond and Arthabaska by Liberal organizers, lor my part I deny them, and I am prepared tomorrow to repeat in the province of Quebec all I have said on this naval affair.

If my good friends find any solace in the remarks of my hon. friend from Dorchester, I have no objection; but it is late in the day for him to deny wha/t he said in Drummond and Arthabaska, when last year on the floor of this House, during the debate on the Address, after having congratulated my hon. friend on his able speech, I said: 'Is it not strange, Mr. Speaker, that my hon. friend has sung "God Save the King," when in the election in Drummond and Arthabaska he used the following words?' I there quoted his words, and he did not deny them. Now that he has passed to the Tory camp for good, now that he has abandoned Mr. Bourassa's principles, my hon. friend find3 a little more courage, and perhaps the office of Solicitor General, which has not yet been filled and which he would adorn, may induce him to be more tolerant of His Majesty the King, and also of His Majesty the Tory party. When my hon. friend made these speeches he did not expect to be reported. He made them with his usual brilliance and eloquence, and I am sorry to say that he carried with him many votes of ignorant people in Drummond and Arthabaska. But it took just a few months for the poor peasants of Drummond and Arthabaska to see through the hybrid combination which was being reared against Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and at the next election they elected my good friend who now represents that constituency in this Parliament (Mr. Brouillard) against Mr. Gilbert.

Was the hon. member
for Drummond and Arthabaska (AH* Brouillard) elected against Mr. Gilbert by those ignorant people to whom my hon. friend made reference?
I see through the little trick. I said a moment ago that the hon. gentleman, by his brilliant speeches, his eloquent words, carried the day with some ignorant people.
No, no.

Yes, he carried the day with some ignorant people. _ But, Sir, if ignorance is bliss for a while, it is not always bliss. Light was restored, more Mr. LEMIEUX*
discussion took place, the people listened and read, and so it happened that at the first opportunity the brave peasantry of the county of Drummond and Arthabaska elected a supporter of the Canadian navy.
My hon. friend has just stated something which is in point. He asks: 'Is it not a fact that Mr. Blondin, the Deputy Speaker, and myself are being taken to task at the present time by Mr. Bourassa? ' I say 'yes,' and I am not surprised at that; but is it not a fact that, by way of retort, in order to explain the situation to the people who elected the Deputy Speaker and my hon. friend from Dorchester, the assertion is made that Mr. Bourassa is wrong in attacking both of these gentlemen -that they have not changed their policies, that Mr. Borden is still with Mr. Bourassa, and that Mr. Bourassa should understand it? Let me quote from the organ of the Deputy Speaker published at Grand Mere.

That is the title of this article published in La Semaine.
How many times-
I am translating.
-during the naval debate has the Liberal party offered to compromise with Mr. Borden? Did not Sir

Wilfrid Laurier say that -we must give $35,000,000-nay, three times, four times $35,000,000, even all the wealth of the country, to help *England? 'I am ready to vote it all, hut let us begin iby building a Canadian navy'?
And, continues the organist:
Mir. Graham, Mr. Guthrie and all the Liberal leaders have renewed the same offer adding also that they were ready to offer the blood of Canadians. Why has Mr. Borden refused the offer of compromise with the Opposition? Why has he -preferred the bitter fight of three months' obstruction? Do you see the alliance?
Let those who lightly treat as cowards and traitors-
That is Mr. Bourassa.
Let those who ligfhly treat as cowards and traitors the hrave French members-
That is the Deputy Speaker and my friend
from Dorchester.
-who have supported the Government; let them pause and reflect a little and let them tell us what would have happened if the fourteen Conservative [Nationalists had banded themselves against the Government.
He will tell us the horrible tale in what follows:
Do they not believe that Mr. Borden, abandoned by his allies, would have been justified to seek an alliance with the Liberals to replace the Nationalists, and do they not see that for fourteen votes lost he would have found to replace them all the Liberals in the House, united to the Conservatives, and the same thing as has happened in the election of Hochelaga would have taken place in the House. The result would have inevitably been the ruin of the Nationalist paz-ty, whose principles Mr. Borden had safeguarded and respected in his Bill as well as in every one of his speeches. Time, the great healer, time will justify those whom Mr. Bourassa condemns so severely.
That is my hon. friend from Dorchester and the Postmaster General:
Time will justify those whom Mr. Bourassa condemns so severely, and the people will learn before long the reasons of profound wisdom which have guided the Quebec members in that dangerous pass. Again, of what does Bourassa complain?
It is true, Mr. Bourassa is condemning the member for Dorchester and the Deputy Speaker very severely, but my hon. friend retorts in his paper, addressing himself to the unfortunate electors who believed in him in 1911:
Of what does Mr. Bourassa complain? But he is all wrong; Mr. Bourasa makes a mistake. Laurier is opposed to Bourassa; Borden, as is shown by his Bill and by his speeches, is his friend, and time will justify our attitude.
There is another article in this very important newspaper, and it is under the suggestive title of : 'Yes, let us suspend armaments.' It does not look like war, it does not look like a very serious naval emergency, if they are going to suspend armaments; the firing line is far away. Shall I translate it all?
Yes.
Dispense.

If I did dispense; it, might help my hon. friends opposite; but, as I am not here to help them but to help the country and the Empire, I shall translate it. It is as follows:
With the adoption of the closure, the agitation about the Naval Aid Bill will stop. Public opinion w-ill be more at ease to judge and to appreciate the object and the hearing of the Naval Bill. It is sufficient to read it to understand that it does not mean sending one red cent to England hut purely and simply to vote a fixed amount which the Government may spend where and when it thinks proper and that even the Government may not spend at all-
That is for Quebec consumption.
-because the Bill does not state any date, any place, and condition and no obligation either.	.
That is right, they have got it down fine.

People who have no interest to get seared of words and who understand that the Cabinet is not obliged to divulge to its opponents its inner thought, will remember the two following considerations in order to know what exactly the condition is.
Here are the two considerations that the Nationalist mind gives out for the Nationalist consumers of Quebec:
_ Though the Laurier Naval Bill was adopted in 1909-1910, a year and a half elapsed before tenders were taken into consideration and at least two more years would have elapsed after they had been accepted before starting to construct ships. Will it be otherwise with the ships that the Borden Government is authorized to construct by the present Bill? Would the Borden Government act otherwise under a law which authorizes it to have the ships in case it will decide to put that law into execution? The Liberals say that the naval yards in England are full 'to the limit and that the construction of the Canadian vessels cannot be started before two years if ever they are ordered. What is clear is this: the Naval Bill is purely and simply a demonstration of friendship to England and nothing else, and should the construction be carried out the law cannot be put into execution before two years; that is to say, before the people have been consulted at a general election. Morally that is all there is in the present law.

With Mr. Bourassa and with. Mr. Christopher West-
The author of that book which has been used so freely during the present debate.
You see, Mr. Chairman, how far fetched it is.
With Mr. Bourassa and with Mr. Christopher West we believe that the next conference of the Hague Tribunal in 1915 will settle forever the principle of armaments, and will sanction the inviolability of trade on the high seas; and, because of that conclusion which we believe is near and inevitable, let us not be scared by the Canadian manifestation of friendship, because it will give us a consultative voice and an influence which nobody can doubt in that great future council of nations. The important thing is that we must not rush into the construction of a navy which we shall be obliged to maintain once it is started; the important thing is to wait, without compromising the situation, until the decision of the Hague Tribunal. Then it will be time to act and to start. Until then, the Government wishes to temporize, to mark time, and the present Bill has no other object. Hysterical people alone can shout: tribute or imperialistic ogre.
This is the literature distributed in the district of Three Rivers and in the district of Quebec, because my hon. friend the Postmaster General has recently in L'Ev&ne-ment an article which bears the same stamp as the two which I have just read. In every concession of the province of Quebec this literature has been distributed by the allies of the right hon. gentleman who leads the Government. Ret no one be bold enough to deny the authenticity, the paternity of such articles, because on another page of the same paper I find a speech delivered by the Deputy Speaker to his political friends at Three Rivers which is headed:
Important Words.-Weighty Words. To a group of important Conservatives of the district of Three Rivers, Mr. Blondin, member for Champlain, was making a few days ago the following declaration which all his friends will read with pleasure and will remember.
Here speaks the Deputy Speaker (Mr. Blondin). '

speechtext: I never gave any interview. I cannot take the responsibility of that.

Mr. LEMIEUX.

I accept of course the
explanation of the Deputy Speaker.
He has not said that he did not say it.
A gentleman is sometimes more truthful in a private conversation than when he speaks before the public. I quite agree that my hon. friend may not have spoken at a meeting.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
